newsitem.title: USA: Florida city turns violent for second time in month.
newsitem.headline: Florida city turns violent for second time in month.

text.p: Small bands of angry youths opened fire at police helicopters and bystanders, injuring at least four people on Wednesday, hours after a grand jury found a white police officer was justified in killing a black motorist last month.

One police officer on the ground was shot in the leg and another in a helicopter said a bullet pierced his shirt sleeve. At least three civilians were also injured in the predominantly poor, black neighbourhood of south St. Petersburg that erupted in sporadic violence, local television reported.
More than 225 police officers on the scene used tear gas to try and disperse the small groups of youths who ran through the streets, throwing bottles, firing weapons and setting fires.
The officer was shot in the leg after police responded to a report of gunfire in the neighbourhood that was rocked by rioting on Oct. 24, St. Petersburg police spokesman Bill Doniel said.

Much of the unrest was centred near the headquarters of a black separatist group, the National Peoples Democratic Uhuru Movement, police said. The group, already under investigation by federal prosecutors for its role in last month's riot, advocates using violence to create a separate black society.
Three members of the group were arrested for minor traffic violations earlier on Wednesday, but authorities insisted there was no connection to the outbreak of violence.

People "are very naive" to believe the violence was the result of the arrests, said Police Chief Darrel Stephens. "We've had threats, constant threats for the past two weeks, saying that if the report from the grand jury didn't meet with their satisfaction that the town was going to burn."
Officer Keith Glasgow, 39, was shot and injured in the left leg.
"He's doing fine," Maj. Cedric Gordon told reporters after a visit to the hospital where Glasgow, an 18-year veteran of the force, was being treated.

Joe Lassen, the co-pilot of a Pinellas County sheriff's helicopter, said one bullet pierced the glass canopy of the aircraft and passed through his shirt sleeve. "We heard the aircraft hit a few times and that was it," he said.

Police stepped up patrols in the neighbourhood after a grand jury ruled Wednesday afternoon that Officer James Knight was justified in the fatal shooting of motorist Tyron Lewis, 18, following a routine traffic stop three weeks ago.

The shooting was followed by hours of rioting in south St. Petersburg. At least 11 people were hurt, mostly police officers, and nearly 30 fires were set in shops, businesses and homes before police regained control of the streets early the next morning.

Black youths in the city charged they were constantly victimised by police. Community leaders said poverty, lack of jobs and bleak prospects for blacks in St. Petersburg created resentment that fuelled last month's unrest.
"We have determined the death of Tyron Lewis was the result of a justifiable homicide under Florida law," Pinellas County State Attorney Bernie McCabe said after the 16-member grand jury acted.
Following the grand jury ruling, the police department suspended Knight for 60 days without pay for violating its firearms policy. Knight's attorney, Joseph Ciarciaglino, said he would appeal.

But the grand jury ruled the death of Lewis was justifiable homicide because Knight was in danger of being run over by the car Lewis was driving after he and his partner, Sandra Minor, pulled Lewis over for speeding.

Knight, 34, appeared before the grand jury on Tuesday to provide his account. He has been on administrative leave since the shooting. Minor, one of the first witnesses to testify in the case, returned on Tuesday to testify a second time.
